bib.title: Chapter 8: Reinforcement Learning and AI Agents (Building AI Agents with LLMs, RAG, and Knowledge Graphs)
bib.venue: Packt book chapter (O'Reilly platform copy, printed 12/26/25)

question: How can an agent learn from interaction with an environment (RL basics, deep RL algorithms, a Super Mario A3C example), and how do LLMs and RL interact?
contributions: Introduces RL fundamentals: bandits, MDPs, Bellman equations, model-free vs model-based, on- vs off-policy.
Summarises DQN, REINFORCE, PPO, actor-critic, AlphaZero.
Walks through an A3C Super Mario Bros agent in PyTorch.
Describes three LLM-RL interaction types: RL-enhanced LLMs, LLM-enhanced RL, combined planning.

results.claim: In the 10-armed bandit demo, a purely greedy agent picks the optimal action only about a third of the time.
results.setup: 10-armed bandit (k=10), true action values drawn from a normal distribution, 1,000 examples plotted; greedy vs epsilon-greedy; no run count or step count stated for the comparison
results.quote: The greedy method chooses the optimal choice only one-third of the time
results.note: Read from Fig 8.8 description; no seeds or number of runs given.

results.claim: In the same bandit demo, epsilon-greedy with epsilon=0.1 selects the optimal action 80% of the time.
results.quote: while a method that includes some exploration selects the optimal choice 80% of the time (ε=0.1)%

results.claim: Too high a constant epsilon (0.5) does worse than pure greedy in the bandit demo.
results.quote: choosing an ε constant that is too high (ε=0.5) leads to worse results than a pure greedy method

results.claim: PPO clips the policy probability ratio to [1-eps, 1+eps]; eps example 0.2.
results.setup: Description of PPO clipped objective; 0.2 is given as an example value (e.g., 0.2)
results.quote: where ϵ is a small hyperparameter (e.g., 0.2), the update is clipped

results.claim: RLHF is described as three steps and PPO is the most popular RL algorithm for it, chosen because the aligned model should stay close to the original.
results.setup: Description, RL-enhanced LLMs section; no experiment
results.quote: collect human feedback data, train a reward model on this data, and conduct fine-tuning of the LLM with RL

limits: The Super Mario example reports no quantitative result (no score, stage cleared rate, training steps, hardware or wall-clock); only a screenshot and a video link.
Bandit figures (8.7-8.11) give no run counts, step counts or seeds in the text.
LLM-RL section is a summary of Cao et al. 2024 (arXiv 2404.00282); no new experiments.
Authors concede A3C is non-deterministic, resource intensive, and relies on CPU parallelism; PPO may suit GPUs better.
Authors concede LLM-enhanced RL inherits LLM bias and hallucination, adds compute and latency cost, and struggles on tasks not in pre-training.
The RLHF/PPO coverage is a few paragraphs: no DPO, GRPO, reward-model details, or verifiable-reward RL.
Final summary states later chapters use LLM agents with tools and no training.
practices: Balance exploration and exploitation; epsilon-greedy, optimistic initial values or UCB beat pure greedy (bandit section).
Define the reward carefully: agents maximise it literally, so a badly specified reward (eating pieces rather than winning chess) yields unintended behaviour (MDP section).
Use a replay buffer and a target network to stabilise DQN (DQN section).
Use PPO's clipped objective to keep policy updates small; tune clip epsilon, learning rate and batch size (PPO section).
Use actor-critic with GAE to lower variance of policy gradients (Super Mario section).
Add an entropy bonus to the loss to encourage exploration (Super Mario section).
Sample actions in training, take the argmax action in evaluation (local_test).
For RLHF, collect human feedback, train a reward model, then fine-tune with RL, usually PPO (RL-enhanced LLMs).
To cut LLM cost in LLM-enhanced RL, use quantization, pruning, small models, mixture of experts or caching (limitations paragraph).
Try PPO or synchronous A2C as easier or more GPU-friendly alternatives to A3C (end of Super Mario section).

terms.definition: a branch of machine learning, where a system must make decisions to maximize cumulative rewards in a given situation
defines how an agent behaves at a certain time; maps the state of the system to an action, can be stochastic or parameterized
the total amount of reward that an agent can expect to get in the future, starting from that state
the model almost always selects the greedy action, but with a probability epsilon it selects one of the other actions
Upper Confidence Bound: non-greedy actions chosen by potential optimality and uncertainty, with c>0 controlling exploration and N the number of times an action was tested
each state summarizes all the previous information; each state possesses all the information needed to predict the future
whether the agent has access to (or learns) a model of the environment
on-policy learns from data of the agent's current policy; off-policy separates behavior policy (collects data) from target policy (learned)
actor learns the policy; critic estimates the value function and supplies a TD error as feedback
information processor, reward designer, decision-maker, generator
